subject: Clarify retention: streaming transcripts vs stored artifacts
messages:
From: Samir Gupta <samir@acmehealth.com>
To: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwoodinference.com>
Date: Sun, 11 Jan 2026 09:12:24 -0800
Subject: Streaming transcript vs stored artifact — retention question

Hi Laura,

Thanks for the demo yesterday. A quick compliance question from our security team: during a live streaming session (where tokens are streamed back to the client), does Redwood persist the intermediate transcript/token stream anywhere by default? Or do we only keep the final generated 'artifact' once the session completes? We need to document what is considered a 'stored artifact' vs transient stream for our SOC 2 evidence.

Specifically:
- Are streamed tokens written to logs or a transient buffer that gets flushed to durable storage?
- If a session is interrupted, is there a tombstone retention or backup snapshot kept anywhere?
- Do attachments (uploads) included in the session get stored separately from the model request/response logs?

Happy to jump on a short call; legal would like written confirmation for the questionnaire.

Thanks,
Samir
Samir Gupta
Head of Platforms, AcmeHealth
samir@acmehealth.com

From: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: Re: Streaming transcript vs stored artifact — retention question

Hi Samir — thanks for the clear list. I pulled together the short answers below and attached two artifacts: a small example session trace (session_trace_example.jsonl) and our high-level retention matrix (redwood_retention_matrix_v1.pdf) for reference.

On Sun, Jan 11, 2026 at 9:12 AM Samir Gupta <samir@acmehealth.com> wrote:
> Thanks for the demo yesterday. A quick compliance question from our security team: during a live streaming session (where tokens are streamed back to the client), does Redwood persist the intermediate transcript/token stream anywhere by default? Or do we only keep the final generated 'artifact' once the session completes? We need to document what is considered a 'stored artifact' vs transient stream for our SOC 2 evidence.
>
> Specifically:
> - Are streamed tokens written to logs or a transient buffer that gets flushed to durable storage?
> - If a session is interrupted, is there a tombstone retention or backup snapshot kept anywhere?
> - Do attachments (uploads) included in the session get stored separately from the model request/response logs?

Short answers (high level):
- Streamed tokens: by default, streaming uses an in-memory buffer; we do not persist intermediate token-by-token streams to durable storage. Only the final assembled response (the generated artifact) is written to the request/response store when the request completes and the call is marked successful.
- Interrupted sessions: when a streaming session is abruptly terminated, the runtime will not commit a final artifact unless the request reaches a terminal state. There is not an automatic durable snapshot of every partial stream; however, operational traces (short-lived debugging traces) may be captured if a customer enables debug mode or opens a support session — those traces are tagged and have their own retention policy.
- Attachments/uploads: user uploads are treated as user-provided objects and are stored in a separate object store (subject to the customer's storage/residency settings). Reference pointers (metadata) may be linked from the request record, but the raw attachment path is managed under the customer's configured storage.

Kimberly (security) — I flagged the two common follow-ups: whether debug traces are captured by default (no) and the specific deletion flow for partial traces (we tombstone metadata and purge content per the retention matrix). Karthik — can you confirm the exact TTLs we should cite in the SOC packet?

Attachments: session_trace_example.jsonl (example, scrubbed), redwood_retention_matrix_v1.pdf

Best,
Laura Bennett

From: Samir Gupta <samir@acmehealth.com>

Date: Sun, 11 Jan 2026 13:20:46 -0800
Subject: Re: Streaming transcript vs stored artifact — retention question

Laura — this is helpful, thank you. Two follow-ups from legal:
1) If there is no durable snapshot of a partial stream, how do you handle backups and disaster recovery? Could a partial stream inadvertently end up in a backup snapshot?
2) For the "tombstone metadata" approach you mentioned — what is the SLA for full purge (i.e., after a customer requests erasure)? Is it an immediate removal from active stores and then background purge from backups, or do you provide timelines?

We need explicit wording for the questionnaire, e.g.: "Intermediate streaming tokens are not stored in durable logs by default; only completed request/response artifacts are committed to storage. In the event of interruption, no durable partial artifacts are retained unless debug capture was explicitly enabled by the customer. Backups are taken at the level of the request store and are subject to deletion timelines described below."

Can you confirm (and if possible provide the exact purge timelines we can include)?

Thanks,
Samir

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik.iyer@redwoodinference.com>

Subject: Re: Streaming transcript vs stored artifact — retention question

Hi Samir — adding the exact language and timelines for the questionnaire below so you can paste directly into your SOC packet. Laura, copying Kimberly for any security edits.

Authoritative wording (recommended):
- Default capture: "By default, Redwood does not persist intermediate streaming tokens to durable logs. Streaming is handled in-memory during request execution; only the final assembled response is committed to the request/response store once the call reaches a terminal state (success or defined error)."
- Debug/diagnostic capture: "If a customer or support session explicitly enables debug/diagnostic capture, short operational traces may be recorded; these traces are marked as diagnostic data and have a separate retention policy (default 30 days) and access controls."
- Interrupted sessions and backups: "Partial streams are not included in standard durable backups. Backups are taken at the request-store level and include only committed, terminal request/response artifacts. In the unlikely event a partial artifact is captured due to debug mode or manual support capture, it is treated as diagnostic data and retained per the diagnostic retention schedule. Backups are encrypted and covered by our disaster recovery process; any customer data in backups is subject to the same deletion workflow described below."
- Erasure/purge SLA: "Upon customer-initiated erasure, Redwood removes entries from the active request/response store within 24 hours. Background purge of tombstoned data from backup snapshots is performed according to our backup lifecycle and typically completes within 90 days; customers requiring accelerated deletion can engage Redwood's Data Erasure playbook documented in the Enterprise SOC packet."

Action items:
- Laura: attach the redlined retention matrix and the scrubbed session trace to the SOC answers (done).
- Kimberly: please confirm the 30/24/90 numbers are acceptable for public documentation or propose edits.
- Samir: let us know if legal wants us to convert the bullets into exact questionnaire answers for upload.

Thanks — happy to hop on a short call if you'd prefer a quick verbal sign-off.
